description: This is a primer on identifying young glossy privet. Look for single-trunked saplings, growing straight as an arrow. Look carefully at the upper surfaces of the leaves. Note the acuminate tip, medium to dark green shiny upper surface, and, except for where leafcutter ants have done their work, entire margins. The leaves are simple and arranged in opposite pairs. Then look at the underside of the leaves. It should be a lighter, dull green, be smooth, and have quite a prominent midvein. At this point, it’s time to examine the entire root system, or at least as much of it as possible. Pull firmly but steadily on the base of the plant, changing direction periodically until the plant comes out of the ground. If in addition to all of the above it has roots, toss it onto a thick network of branches of comparable size. If it and its roots remain aboveground, it’s a glossy privet. Excellent work!

description: Girdled 4/14/18, this privet is showing why this is not the best time of year to girdle them. Even when the surface is scraped clean, new tissue forms throughout the girdled gap. Left to itself, this tree would reconnect its bark—and, more to the point, its phloem—in a matter of weeks. We can prevent that from happening if we come back and scrape it clean every week or two until it stops adding new tissue. Because this tissue is still moist 2 weeks after the girdling was done, it will definitely produce new bark and phloem in the next few weeks if we were to leave it alone.

description: This series of photos shows that glossy privet starts taking over the forest from the instant it sprouts. The first two show that beneath the canopy of a mature privet its seedlings sprout densely. From either top or side, privet is almost all you see. In those first two photos, look for a small white dot. It’s just to the right of center near the bottom of the first photo, and it’s a little less than a quarter of the way into the picture from the center of the right side of the second photo. That marks the spot of a white avens (Geum canadense), which is one of two plants left in the 13.5-inch-square plot from which I pulled the 35 seedlings and saplings of glossy privet shown in the other photos. (That’s one of my size 14s in each direction.) In the last photo, you can see that white avens next to my foot, with a greenbrier (Smilax bona-nox) next to it. Arching in from outside the plot is an elbowbush (Forestiera pubescens; also called stretchberry). The density of privets is about 250 to the square yard, or about 300 per square meter—about twice the number I’ve found in previous less precise measurements.

description:
This is the same champion (invasive) privet tree that I previously documented here:
https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/19821907
The present observation documents the next phase of tree removal that I started in late August.  You will see how I took my chainsaw and girdled the right hand trunk at about 3 and 4 ft above ground (where it was easy to reach with the chainsaw).  I have subsequently sprayed and poured almost two quarts of concentrated vinegar on the exposed cut surfaces to destroy the vascular tissue above and below the cut.  Time will tell if I have succeeded in killing this half of the tree.
(Removing this entire tree in one operation is not an option due to some particulars of it location and the danger of such an effort to surrounding native trees and vegetation.)
UPDATE: More on the story of the removal of this tree can be found here:

description:
I took a hike in our neighborhood park to examine the damage from the mid-February ice/snow storm and cold snap.  The damage is massive, but I wanted to emphasize one aspect that will be intriguing to watch over the next several months (and years).  The 10-day freeze caused the vast majority of the Glossy Privets to lose their leaves.  I need to emphasize that this is one of the hardiest evergreen invasive species we've been dealing with for years in the park.  The leaves are tough and leathery...and NOT deciduous.  But this freeze killed 95-99% of the foliage on all the Glossy Privets.
   I can't tell yet if some/any of the trees themselves have died back.  Given my long-continuing battles with this species, I'm expecting almost all of the individual trees to resprout either from the trunks or bases.  It will be quite ugly.
The upside of all this damage to the privet is that, at least temporarily, the native understory and ground cover species will be receiving additional sunlight.  You can see in the last image how a young stand of privet, formerly a dense shaded thicket, has now been opened up.  Time will tell what overall changes to the park's vegetation will have occurred.

description:
Here is the latest documentation of the slow demise of this champion Glossy Privet.  Previous documentation of this individual tree can be seen here:
Jan 2015: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/19821907
Aug 2019: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/32991205 by which time one of three major trunks had been felled and a 2nd one had been girdled.

The canopy foliage of that 2nd (girdled) trunk finally died in 2020.  Then the extreme cold weather in mid-February 2021 killed the canopy foliage of the remaining large trunk.  The first image here shows most of the 60-ft tree.  The right side of the tree is the standing dead trunk--now two years dead, and the trunk cut through about 1/2 way but it's still standing.  Most of the leafy foliage in the "canopy" on the left of the tree is actually that of a couple of Heart-leaf Ampelopsis vines (*Ampelopsis cordata*) which had climbed into the tree.  But in the center of the tree, against the blue sky and white clouds, you can see some 8 to 10-ft long sprouts of new growth from this year just since the freeze.  So the left trunk of the tree was top-killed but still lives; it has not been girdled yet.
The second image shows a healthy stand of Frostweed (*Verbesina virginica*; also uploaded as a separate observation) which has colonized the formerly heavily-shaded ground under this giant Ligustrum.  "Nature abhors a vacuum."  (The blue rope cordons off an area to the left of the tree which is a hazard zone due to the impending fall of another major branch of the tree.)
The third image shows the current status of the trunks of the tree: One (in front) gone; a second one thoroughly girdled and mostly cut through, and the third one (on left) still intact.  The latter trunk will be girdled soon.
The fourth photo shows a typical reaction from Ligustrums like this.  With the death of the canopy of this huge tree (3-ft basal diameter), the tree puts out abundant root and stump sprouts in an attempt to regrow.  Happily, deer browse on these new sprouts heavily, but I also come by periodically and either break these off or spray them with vinegar to kill the sprouts, all in an effort to use up the energy stored in the massive root system of this individual.
UPDATE (May 31, 2022): The final chapter in the removal of this tree can be found here:
https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/119774360

description: This tree was girdled 13 months before Winter Storm Uri. It was Mostly Dead when Uri hit. Before the root system had died, Uri killed the top. We will have to figure out how to kill this privet and others that were girdled at the same time—perhaps prune back the shoots to a half dozen or so, let them grow for a year or two, and then girdle them.

description:
Here's the latest and perhaps last documentation for the saga of a "champion" Glossy Privet that was on my back slope.  The last of the two remaining trunks finally died after the "snow-pocalypse" of 2021 and rotten branches were beginning to fall down in wind storms piecemeal.  So I hired a professional crew to bring down the remnants of the tree.  The first image shows the dead standing trunks on the morning of the tree's final demise.  The 2nd image shows the outcome of the crew's work.  Now I'm left with several piles of sticks and lumber and a nice flat stump that we can use as a picnic table (3rd image).  Previous documentation of this giant invader can be seen here:
https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/19821907
https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/32991205

description:
I had a feeling it was invasive, because it just didn't seem to "fit" in the landscape, but I was surprised that it came out to privet because it looks so different from the privet that I am used to -- the leaves are much bigger and evergreen.

The key in Petrides (1972):

Simple, opposite leaves

1 . Erect trees and shrubs:
  2 . Leaves not toothed, although sometimes wavy-edged:
    3. Leaves not heart-shaped:
       4 . Papery scales not present at twig bases:
          6 . Leaves with veins only slightly, if at all, following the leaf edges:
             9 . Buds otherwise [i.e., not Viburnum]; bundle scars 1-3; evergreen or not:
                MISCELLANEOUS

This narrowed it down to Kalmia, Ligustrum, Cephalanthus, Borrichia, Calycanthus, Chionanthus, Osmanthus, Buckleya, Nestronia,  Decodon, Symphoricarpos, Hypericum, Shepherdia, or Leiophyllum. All except Ligustrum were easily ruled out by reading the individual descriptions.

This invasive privet is present in lesser numbers than the ubiquitous Chinese privet (see observation https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/146358298).
